## The question, frozen

**What:** under the CONSORT rule, what must a report of a randomised controlled trial say, item by item, and why is each item needed?
**Range:** primary reports of two-group parallel RCTs (the document says so; extensions are named for other designs).
**Asked:** a *rule/definition* question ("what counts as adequate reporting?") with a *purpose* question bolted to it ("does reporting it achieve the aim of letting readers judge validity?"). The title and abstract make this central, so I freeze this and not the neighbouring question of whether trials were well run.

## The explanation in parts

Its parts are: the framing premise (reports are deficient and deficiencies track bias); the checklist items; the flow diagram; the good-reporting examples; and the causal claim (adopting CONSORT improves reports).

## Part by part

| Part | Mark | Held by / note |
|---|---|---|
| 1a word "randomised" in title | **Held if** | Holds only if "indexers may not classify" is true — asserted, uncited. What would settle it: indexers shown the same abstracts with and without the word. |
| 1b structured abstract | **Held if** | Held only by "some studies have found" — not named. |
| 2a rationale, 2b objectives | **Held** | Ethics job (Helsinki; don't repeat an answered question). |
| 3a design description | **Held** | Generalisability/interpretation job. |
| 3b changes to methods | **Held** | The unexplained-discrepancy evidence. |
| 4a eligibility, 4b settings | **Held** | Applicability job. |
| 5 interventions | **Held** | Replication job. |
| 6a outcomes, 6b outcome changes | **Held** | Outcome-switching evidence (62% changed a primary outcome). |
| 7a sample size | **Held** | Power-interpretation job. |
| 7b interim analyses | **Held** | The false-positive arithmetic (19% vs 5%). |
| 8a sequence generation | **Held** | Bias evidence. |
| 8b restriction/blocking | **Held** | But pulls (below). |
| 9 allocation concealment | **Held** | Strongest of all: larger effects where concealment was inadequate. |
| 10 who generated/enrolled/assigned | **Held if** | Mechanism argued ("the generator could keep a copy"), no citation. Settle by a case where the roles were split. |
| 11a blinding, 11b similarity | **Held** | Bias evidence; and an internal flip used well (see below). |
| 12a statistics, 12b extra analyses | **Held** | Verification job; multiplicity evidence. |
| 13a/13b flow diagram | **Held** | Reporting was better in articles that had one. |
| 14a recruitment dates | **Borrowed** | Rests on the general claim that therapy evolves and changes routine care — not tested here. |
| 14b why the trial stopped | **Held** | Early-stopping evidence. |
| 15 baseline table | **Held** | And it rules out a named rival (baseline significance tests are "illogical"). |
| 16 numbers analysed | **Held** | The carotid-stenosis contrast: per-protocol and intention-to-treat disagreed. |
| 17a/17b results, absolute+relative | **Held** | Selective-reporting evidence. |
| 18 other analyses | **Held** | Multiplicity argument. |
| 19 harms | **Held** | Balance job. |
| Tail sentence: harms may come from the condition | **Borrowed** | Rests on trial causal-inference, untested here. |
| Framing premise (deficiencies → bias) | **Held** | Cited (concealment, intention-to-treat). |
| Causal claim (CONSORT → better reports) | **Loose** | Only an association. Near neighbour that would do as well: journals that enforce reporting anyway. |

## Whole-explanation checks

**Flip.** For most items the opposite would not have been recommended, so the items are not just-so. The document's own best flip is internal: it *removed* the advice to report blinding-tests, after flipping showed those answers cannot separate failed blinding from a good guess. That is the method done by the authors.

**Direction.** The evidence-backed items run forward (deficiency plus bias → report it). But the *list as a whole* runs backward from the aim: "readers cannot judge validity without transparent reporting, therefore report these items." For every item whose evidence was not supplied, the answer was already sitting in that starting point. That is the single most useful finding here.

**Pulls.** Three named joints. (1) Reporting block size aids transparency but "could lead to code breaking" — the line is drawn in favour of reporting. (2) Protocol changes "should be made without breaking the blinding". (3) Abstract completeness against journal word limits — resolved by prescribing content, not format. Each pull names where it gives way.

**Patches and catch-alls, with gauges.** "Extensions" for other designs (gauge: a design-specific checklist). "Modified intention-to-treat" dropped in favour of exactly who was included (gauge: a clear description). "Usual care" must be described thoroughly (gauge: the description). These are catch-alls *carrying* gauges — good practice, not a dodge.

**Change list.** It covers primary parallel two-group reports and openly leaves out ethics approval, consent, data monitoring committees and cost-effectiveness. Declared up front, so a limit, not a silent narrowing.

**Rivals.** The rival for *why* reporting is poor — weak incentives and no enforcement — is not ruled out anything the document contains. Its causal claim survives only as correlation.

**Where the parts came from.** *Built:* the concealment/blinding split, and dropping the explicit intention-to-treat question. *Fitted:* the chosen "good reporting" examples and the block-size advice. *Asserted:* the indexing claim, the structured-abstract superiority, "CONSORT is not a quality instrument."

## What would make it harder to vary

1. Give each held-if item its contrast: a measurable read-out where the item's presence or absence predicts usability or bias. Three items carry the most weight on the least evidence — the title word, structured abstracts, recruitment dates.
2. Test the causal claim directly: journals allocated to adopt CONSORT or not, with outcomes written down first. That would kill or keep the enforcement rival.

## What this does not show

Hard to vary is not true. Passing does not show that following the checklist produces valid trials, only that most items are held in place by something checkable.

## One next step

For the three held-if items, write the two halves of a poke each — one change that should matter, one that should not — then look for that change in the literature before patching anything.
